title: How AI-era disinformation targets both human and machine cognition
gist: Agentic AI and coordinated 'AI swarms' are expanding disinformation from targeting human belief to also poisoning machine cognition (training data, model outputs), creating corporate risks like deepfake-driven stock manipulation and demanding new defenses such as sovereign models and mechanistic interpretability.

themes.theme: Scale of synthetic content flooding the information ecosystem

insights.claim: An estimated 50% of newly published articles are now AI-generated, and synthetic content appears on up to 74% of new webpages, blurring the line between human- and machine-generated content.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Business intelligence and analytics inputs sourced from the open web are increasingly synthetic, degrading signal quality for research and due diligence that relies on scraped content.
insights.quote: An estimated 50% of newly published articles are now AI-generated, while synthetic content appears on up to 74% of new webpages.
insights.locator: Since 2022, generative AI, particularly large language models

insights.claim: Low-cost, multi-modal LLMs have lowered the barrier to entry for malicious actors, enabling text, audio and video disinformation at scale, and recent deepfakes are now convincing enough to be exploited for political and financial gain (unlike easily-spotted early deepfakes).
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Falling cost of convincing synthetic media raises the base rate of fraud and market-manipulation attempts that security and compliance teams must screen for.
insights.quote: Low-cost, multi-modal LLMs have lowered the barrier to entry for malicious actors, enabling text, audio and video disinformation at scale.
insights.locator: Influence operations have long used disinformation, evolving as technology has

themes.theme: Agentic AI and AI swarms as disinformation infrastructure

insights.claim: An estimated 28.6 million AI agents were in use across enterprises in 2025, a figure projected to exceed 2 billion by 2030, indicating explosive growth of autonomous systems that operate with limited human oversight.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The scale-up of enterprise AI agents (28.6M to 2B+ in five years) implies a rapidly expanding attack surface for coordinated misuse, relevant to cybersecurity and AI-governance vendors.
insights.quote: An estimated 28.6 million agents were in use across enterprises in 2025, and this is projected to exceed 2 billion by 2030.
insights.locator: Agentic AI adds complexity to this threat landscape

insights.claim: When specialized AI agents operate in coordinated networks or 'swarms,' they can amplify disinformation through greater autonomy, sophistication, scale and speed than rule-bound bots, enabling adaptive end-to-end influence operations once a goal is set with little human oversight.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: AI swarms represent a qualitatively new disinformation vector distinct from legacy bot networks; detection systems built for rule-bound bots may not catch adaptive swarm behavior.
insights.quote: Unlike rule-bound bots, agentic AI may enable adaptive, end-to-end influence operations with little human oversight once a goal is set.
insights.locator: The risk compounds when specialized AI agents operate in coordinated networks

insights.claim: In a USC study using a simulated social media environment, 500 AI agents independently coordinated to promote a political candidate, demonstrating that agent-driven influence campaigns are already technically feasible, not merely hypothetical.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Empirical proof-of-concept for autonomous coordinated influence operations should accelerate demand for AI-driven detection tools and inform regulatory timelines.
insights.quote: In a simulated social media environment created as part of a recent USC study, 500 AI agents independently coordinated to promote a political candidate.

insights.claim: Agent-driven disinformation campaigns used against businesses or public figures could inflict reputational damage within days, even though trust takes years to build.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The asymmetry between rapid reputational destruction and slow trust-building argues for investing in real-time brand-monitoring and rapid-response crisis capabilities rather than relying on legacy PR response times.
insights.quote: such agent-driven campaigns could inflict reputational damage within days where trust takes years to build.

themes.theme: Corporate and market risk from disinformation

insights.claim: Companies face exposure through supply chains and market manipulation via coordinated disinformation targeting stock-sensitive news or deepfakes impersonating executives, and this risk should be on every board's radar.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Boards and risk committees should treat deepfake-driven market manipulation as an enterprise risk category alongside cyber and supply-chain risk, prompting demand for executive-impersonation detection and verification protocols.
insights.quote: Companies face exposure through supply chains and market manipulation via coordinated disinformation on stock-sensitive news or deepfakes impersonating executives. This should be on every board's radar.
insights.locator: Companies face exposure through supply chains

insights.claim: Malicious actors' motives split between extortion/fraud and subversion (exploiting political and social vulnerabilities to undermine established authority), with subversion sitting at the heart of the emerging practice of 'cognitive warfare' that targets how people and institutions make sense of reality and decisions.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Distinguishing financially-motivated disinformation from subversion-motivated cognitive warfare helps risk teams prioritize different defenses (fraud controls vs. narrative/decision-integrity monitoring).
insights.quote: Where disinformation manipulates the narrative, cognitive warfare seeks to influence how people, companies, institutions and societies make sense of reality and make decisions.

themes.theme: Machine cognition as an attack surface

insights.claim: Cognitive warfare in the AI era can target machine cognition directly, not just human belief, via data poisoning of the systems that increasingly perceive, infer and reason.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: AI models themselves become a target class requiring security investment (data provenance, poisoning defenses), not just an amplification tool for attacking humans.
insights.quote: cognitive warfare can also target machine cognition – processes in artificial systems resembling human perception, inference and reasoning.

insights.claim: 'LLM grooming' — planting deceptive content across the open web so it enters training data and skews model outputs — is a known attack technique, and one study found just 250 poisoned documents are enough to embed a hidden vulnerability into an LLM.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A surprisingly low poisoning threshold (250 documents) means training-data curation and provenance verification are cheap-to-attack, high-value defense priorities for any org fine-tuning or deploying LLMs.
insights.quote: one study showing that 250 poisoned documents are enough to embed a hidden vulnerability into an LLM.
insights.locator: LLM grooming can plant deceptive content

insights.claim: As human-generated data grows scarce and models increasingly train on synthetic data, this risks self-reinforcing errors and biases, a phenomenon known as 'model collapse,' and AI swarms could fill data voids early with synthetic content to distort public perception before credible information exists.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Model collapse and data-void exploitation are structural risks to AI training pipelines that argue for sourcing verified/proprietary data rather than open-web scrapes as synthetic content share rises.
insights.quote: As human-generated data grows scarce, models increasingly train on synthetic data, risking self-reinforcing errors and biases. This phenomenon is known as model collapse.

insights.claim: Evidence suggests AI interactions can shift beliefs across contested societal issues, making AI models themselves high-value targets whose compromise risks contaminating both machine and human cognition and the judgement underlying public- and private-sector decisions.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If AI outputs measurably move human opinion, model integrity becomes a systemic input to decision-making across sectors, elevating AI trust/safety as a governance and investment priority.
insights.quote: Evidence suggests AI interactions can shift beliefs across contested societal issues. AI models thus present high-value targets.

insights.claim: Regulation needs to address the systemic incentives that favour disinformation, including its lower production cost relative to truthful content and digital platforms' tendency to prioritize engagement over accuracy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Policy interventions that target platform incentive structures (engagement-optimized ranking) rather than only content takedown may be more durable levers against disinformation economics.
insights.quote: regulation must address accountability and alter the systemic incentives that favour disinformation, such as its lower production cost relative to truthful content as well as the tendency of digital platforms to prioritise engagement over accuracy.
insights.locator: On the human side, individual, institutional and societal resilience

insights.claim: Sovereign or in-house models trained on trusted, verified datasets reduce exposure to data poisoning and model collapse, and progress in mechanistic interpretability — understanding models' inner workings — would enable better tracing and auditing of AI behaviour.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investment thesis angle: demand for sovereign/proprietary LLM infrastructure and interpretability tooling is likely to grow as organizations seek to de-risk data-poisoning exposure.
insights.quote: Sovereign or in-house models trained on trusted, verified datasets reduce exposure to data poisoning and model collapse.
insights.locator: As AI systems become part of global cognitive infrastructure

insights.claim: Defensive AI agents could detect disinformation by identifying coordination patterns unlikely to be human, and could monitor brand reputation to flag defamation campaigns before they gain traction; cross-platform monitoring also shows promise in predicting how false narratives spread.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Points to an emerging market for AI-vs-AI defensive tooling — coordination-pattern detection and cross-platform narrative monitoring — as a countermeasure category to agentic disinformation.
insights.quote: defensive AI agents could detect disinformation by identifying coordination patterns that are unlikely to be human. They could also monitor brand reputation to flag defamation campaigns before they gain traction.

insights.claim: AI swarms exploit a deepening 'epistemic crisis' in which traditional intermediaries such as science, media and government agencies have seen their authority decline with the rise of the internet and social media, weakening collective trust and leaving societies more susceptible to disinformation.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Declining institutional trust is a pre-existing structural vulnerability that agentic disinformation exploits, meaning technical fixes alone (detection tools) are insufficient without institutional trust-rebuilding.
insights.quote: AI swarms meet fertile ground amid what some call a deepening epistemic crisis due to the erosion of society's ability to agree on fundamental facts.
